summary: For ages 5–7, Moon phases is purely an observational-pattern topic: children watch the Moon change shape over about a month, learn to name a few phases (new/dark, half, full; 'growing' and 'shrinking'), and recognise that the shapes repeat in a predictable cycle. The causal explanation (reflected sunlight, Sun–Earth–Moon geometry) is deliberately deferred to a later orbit topic, because introducing geometry now tends to entrench the wrong 'Earth's shadow' story. The core work is careful, repeated observation and the noticing of a repeating pattern, with a predict-then-check rhythm. Phase vocabulary is built alongside the observing.
misconceptions: The Moon's phases are caused by clouds covering part of it, or by Earth's shadow falling on it (avoid seeding this; the real cause is taught later — keep to observing the pattern)
The Moon changes shape randomly / has no pattern (it repeats in a predictable ~monthly cycle)
A new Moon means there is no Moon there at all (it is still there but we can't see the lit part)
The different phases are different Moons (it is the same Moon looking different at different times)
The Moon changes shape within a single night (the change is slow, from night to night over a month)

activities.title: Month-long Moon diary
steps: For about a month, whenever you can see the Moon, draw its shape (at home with a family member helping). The Moon is not up in the evening every night: around new Moon you won't see it at all, and in the 'shrinking' part of the month it rises late, so look for it in the early-morning or daytime sky (never at the Sun). On days you can't see it, write 'not seen'.
Note the date beside each drawing so the record stays in order.
At the end, lay all the drawings out in sequence — a strip or a circle — and look for how the shape changes night to night.
Point to where the Moon grows from a thin sliver to a full round circle, and where it shrinks back down again.
Say out loud what you notice: 'it got thinner', 'tonight it's a full Moon', 'it will grow again'.
activities.insight: The Moon's shape changes slowly from night to night over about a month, and the shapes repeat in the same order again and again — it is a predictable pattern, not random.

activities.title: Fast-forward the month and guess tomorrow
steps: Drag a slider across about 29 nights and watch the Moon in the window fatten from a thin sliver to a full bright circle, then thin back down to nothing.

After watching a week or two, switch to a 'guess the next night' mode: the next few Moon shapes are hidden — use the direction you have just seen (growing or shrinking) to pick the shape you think comes next.
Drag on to reveal the real shape and check your guess.
Optionally stamp your own real Moon-diary drawings into the strip so your night-time observations and the tool tell the same story.
activities.insight: Because the growing-then-shrinking rhythm repeats, once you have watched which way the Moon is heading you can predict what it will look like next — the shapes follow a pattern you can rely on.

activities.title: Name and order the phases
steps: Use a phase strip or wheel: tap or turn to each phase and hear or read its child-friendly name (new/dark, half, full).
Match each phase picture or photo to its name.
Answer 'what comes after full?' by lifting a flap or saying the next shape.
Put a jumbled set of the month's shapes back into the right order.
Say which comes next when shown part of the sequence.
activities.insight: A few phases have names (new/dark, half, full), and they always come in the same order, so you can say what follows a given shape.

activities.title: Predict-and-explain check: will the sliver change?
steps: Consider: tonight the Moon looks like a thin curved sliver. Over the next two weeks, will it stay the same shape or change?
Say what you think it will do — and, importantly, how you know; use what your diary or recent nights have shown about whether the Moon has lately been growing or shrinking.
Talk through what you'd expect after the Moon becomes a full round circle.
activities.insight: Over two weeks the Moon will definitely change — it will not stay a sliver. Which way it heads (toward full if it has been growing, or toward new if it has been shrinking) is read from the recent trend, and justified by the repeating monthly cycle rather than by the weather.

checkQuestion: Tonight the Moon looks like a thin curved sliver. Over the next two weeks, will it stay that same shape or change? What do you think it will do — and HOW do you know?
checkAnswer: It will change. The Moon slowly changes shape over about a month, growing from a thin sliver to a full round circle and then shrinking back to a sliver again, and this same pattern repeats over and over. So over two weeks the thin sliver will grow towards a fuller, rounder Moon. We know because the Moon goes through the same repeating cycle of shapes every month.
